In the three included RCTs, heterogeneity increased, and the pooled Risk Ratio for ORR was 1.31 (95% CI: 0.58–2.98), crossing 1 (not statistically significant).', 'relevance': "Provides context on why Phase III data is needed; current RCT evidence is insufficient to establish efficacy, reinforcing the gap's importance."}] This review article systematically catalogs clinical trials of FMT combined with ICIs in solid tumors (Table 1), listing 29 trials with their phases, tumor types, and primary outcomes. All listed trials are Phase I, Phase Ib, Phase I/II, or Phase II; none are Phase III. The review explicitly states in Section 5.1 that 'large-scale, multi-center randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are essential to comprehensively evaluate the therapeutic potential of FMT in augmenting ICI therapy,' identifying this as a future research direction rather than completed evidence. The review discusses one randomized controlled trial (NCT03817125, SER-401) that was modified from a four-arm to a two-arm placebo-controlled design, but this was not Phase III and showed lower response rates in the intervention group versus placebo. The review provides mechanistic explanations for heterogeneous trial results (microbiota composition, metabolites, TME remodeling, signaling pathways) and outlines what future Phase III trials should measure (OS, PFS, ORR, quality of life). This study explicitly characterizes the current evidence level for fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) as predominantly derived from early-phase, single-arm studies. It identifies a 2026 phase 2 randomized controlled trial (TACITO trial in metastatic renal cell carcinoma) as a pivotal step but notes it did not formally meet its primary endpoint. The authors conclude that large-scale phase 3 randomized controlled trials are critically needed and urgently prioritized to validate efficacy across tumor types, implying their absence in the published literature up to March 2026. The text also summarizes efficacy outcomes from available phase 1/2 trials (e.g., ORR of 80% in NSCLC, 75% in melanoma, 43% pooled in solid tumors) to contextualize the need for higher-level evidence.
